findings.title: Hoped-for aid turns into opposition
findings.claim: The focus can be read as a reversal of expected support: the worshipped beings disavow the worship relation and become a contrary party against those who took them as strength. The wider wording at 36:74–75 makes hoped-for aid and its failure explicit, while 46:6 repeats worship-disavowal and enmity at the gathering.
findings.mechanism: The governed complement بِعِبَادَتِهِمْ ties ك ف ر to a particular worship relation rather than generic disbelief; the عَلَيْهِمْ phrase gives the contrary predicate a target. At 36:74 the adopted powers are taken in hope of aid, and 36:75 says they cannot help; 46:6 pairs enmity with disavowal of worship at the gathering. These distinct wider triggers return through the focus's repudiation, worship, and opposition carriers, turning failed aid into active relational rejection.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can trace a full relational turn: aid is sought, the worship bond is disowned, and the focus ends with the parties facing one another as adversaries; 46:6 makes that turn visible at the gathering.
findings.containment: The trusted cross-run strength framing is retained as an attributed reading, while the focus packet does not settle one referent for its plural subject and attached pronouns. The external verses are semantic parallels; their morphology is not imported. The opposition here does not by itself assert physical combat or identify every party in the wider scene.

epistemic.reason: Accepted focus branches and the supplied Arabic in 36:74–75 and 46:6 support the relational reversal. The cross-run source is trusted, but the plural antecedents remain open and connection targets lack supplied morphology.
